Even that is not true. The minister cannot get away with that nonsense.
I rise today on this question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, not to ask the house to set my word against the word of hon. gentlemen opposite or vice versa but simply because there is a record of what went on in the special committee on procedure, and I want to refer to that record. I have in my hand the minutes of two of the meetings of that committee, and they make it clear that my statement was correct. I will not take the time of the house to read these minutes in full, but I believe I am entitled to refer to them. I am not referring to several days when we made incidental references to this question, or days when we were told this was the problem we would have to deal with before we got through with our business.
At any rate, the record or minutes of the committee show that on Tuesday, November 26, at a full dress meeting, after a few preliminaries the greater part of the meeting-in fact four pages of minutes-had to do with the question of the programming of house business. The minutes indicate that some of us objected to any idea of putting the matter completely in the hands of the government. In the minutes this sentence is to be found on page 2:
Mr. Macdonald said that he had to insist on a residual power being given to the government.
It is reported that Mr. Macdonald went on to say that his colleagues would expect him to put through a certain program of legislation, and the reserve or residual power would be needed to ensure this. Two pages later in the minutes the point is reached where the committee agreed to instruct the clerk of the committee to prepare a paper for referral to the draftsman as follows-and there are a number of points which indicate the things we were all agreed on; namely, that there was to be a proceedings committee; that it was to hold meetings; that it was to have a chairman and so many members, and so on; but that it was to act, so far as these parts of the proposal were concerned, only on the basis of a unanimous decision.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
At that point the minutes said, quite correctly, that the President of the Privy Council

December 16, 1968
Discussion of Procedure said he would prepare a draft dealing with cases when there was disagreement in the business committee.
That was on Tuesday, November 26, and I say practically the whole of that meeting was devoted to a very thorough discussion of this whole matter even before there was a draft in front of us.
Then the minutes of Tuesday, December 2, will show that we met at 8.30 p.m. in room 112N and did not adjourn until 10.30 that night. It is recorded that a draft of 16A was placed before us. In fact there were two drafts, one which had been prepared by the clerk of the committee at our request and another prepared by the President of the Privy Council which went much further and was more or less along the lines of the proposal in the report which was finally made.
The minutes of the committee include a report of the statements made by several of the members of the committee. For example, I am quoted as saying that the question of programming business was one which had constitutional overtones. I said parliament was a place of debate and there were certain ground rules which had always been observed. I said I still had faith in co-operation and consultation and believed that a proceedings committee would be able to agree on the programming of business without an ultimate sanction. Later, as the minutes say, I made it clear that in my view such a rule would be detrimental to parliament and that no government had the right to take such powers.
The discussion went on, and among those taking part in it were the hon. member for Edmonton West, the hon. member for Sudbury, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Peace River. Finally the chairman indicated that since we .were in disagreement the only thing to do was to take a vote, and each clause was called separately. The minutes say that Mr. Lambert recorded his dissent on section 1, Mr. Knowles on section 2, minor drafting changes were incorporated in section 3, changes were made in section 4, and so on. Mr. Macdonald, seconded by Mr. Jerome, then moved that the proposed standing order as amended be adopted for inclusion as a recommendation in the report of the committee. On this question the committee divided:	yeas, Messrs. Deachman,
Forest, Jerome, Lang, Macdonald; nays, Messrs. Baldwin, Fairweather, Knowles, Lambert. The minutes show that the vote

represented a straight division between hon. members on the government side and hon. members of the opposition.
Surely in the light of this record it is clear that we did discuss this subject at length for two full meetings. This is a controversial question, and I submit that for the minister to say he was advised-

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-143, intituled "An Act to amend the Meat Inspection Act (Inspection Legend)".

subtopic: PROVISION THAT GRADE STAMP BE IN BOTH LANGUAGES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION THAT GRADE STAMP BE IN BOTH LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time when all Canadians seem to unite in promoting bilingualism and biculturalism, it seems to me appropriate to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the importance of this bill, which was already introduced on January 22, 1968 as Bill No. C-196.
Section 68 of the regulations under the act provides that the stamp put on inspected meat shall be in English only. Consequently, this bill stipulates that the stamp shall henceforth be in the two official languages and that it shall bear the same maple leaf as the Canadian flag.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO COUNTY AND DISTRICT COURTS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-144, to amend the Divorce Act.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO COUNTY AND DISTRICT COURTS
speechtext:
Explain.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)

subtopic: EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO COUNTY AND DISTRICT COURTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to confer a concurrent jurisdiction on the county and district courts of provinces other than Quebec and Newfoundland in divorce matters. Under the bill for divorce which was passed at the last session, jurisdiction was given to the supreme courts alone of the provinces. It has been found in experience, exactly as had been anticipated by some of us, that the supreme court is being clogged with a great load of actions for divorce resulting in delay, the holding up of cases, and the courts being unable to do their work. The purpose of this bill is to give concurrent jurisdiction to county and district courts, which incidentally will make the proceedings less expensive.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

RESPONSIBILITY IN DEATH OF GIRL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave), to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance, namely the death of a young native Indian girl on highway No. 1 just west of Brandon, Manitoba, early this month and the guilt of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in respect of her death.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY IN DEATH OF GIRL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The hon. member knows that he must address the Chair on the question of urgency of debate, and I think it would be helpful at least to the house, if not to the Chair, for the hon. member to make his contribution at this stage in respect of the question of urgency, which is the only matter that can be before the house at this moment.

subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY IN DEATH OF GIRL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Yes, indeed, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that is the main question and that the other one ancillary to it is the propriety of setting aside the other public business in order to have such a debate.
If I may be permitted perhaps I might briefly outline the circumstances leading to the death of this girl, who was 21 or 22 years of age. Perhaps this would help put the matter in perspective. What I intend to say involves what I consider to be guilt on the part of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, even though there
Responsibility in Girl's Death was action on the part of a particular superintendent of an Indian agency, who was only putting into effect what I consider to be the generally casual, administratively inefficient and, worst of all, indifferent attitude which exists on the part of the department. The superintendent's actions only reflect that casualness and indifference.
The young girl in question was from the Oak River Indian reserve near Griswold, Manitoba. She had been committed to the Pine Grove correctional centre in Saskatchewan for the offence of assault committed in the province of Saskatchewan. The sentencing magistrate, having some compassion, made a notation on the warrant of committal to the effect that the young girl was from outside the province and that some arrangement should be made in respect of her before her release date.
The superintendent of the Pine Grove correctional centre, after receiving the warrant of committal, contacted the John Howard Society in Prince Albert, which in turn wrote to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development at Brandon, Manitoba, pointing out in the letter the date of her release, the desire and need she had for educational upgrading and trades training, with a specific request to the agency to assist her with transportation from Moosomin, Saskatchewan to her home about 50 or 60 miles from Brandon, Manitoba. I suppose because the province of Saskatchewan is unable constitutionally to provide money for such a trip outside the jurisdiction of that province, the superintendent of the Indian agency in Brandon replied suggesting that with regard to transportation the young girl should contact some of her relatives on the Oak River reserve, requesting that they meet her at Moosomin. The superintendent said in his letter that most of the Indians on the Oak River reserve had automobiles and no doubt would meet her there.
When the young girl was released from the Pine Grove correctional centre at Prince Albert she had approximately $2 in her possession and fully believed that she would have to hitchhike from Moosomin, Saskatchewan to her home close to Griswold, Manitoba. She had no other means of transportation.
Unknown to her the Indian superintendent on his own, without notifying this young girl or the John Howard Society at Prince Albert, had made arrangements for relatives to pick her up at Moosomin, without indicating the time of the arrival of the bus or anything of that nature. The young girl left Prince Albert
December 16. 1968

Responsibility in Girl's Death by bus at about nine in the morning. The next that was heard about her was just after midnight, at 12.45 a.m. following the date of her release, when the R.C.M.P. at Brandon received a call from a farmer that a girl's body had been found on the highway about six miles west of Brandon. She had a blood alcohol content of 0.283, which indicates a state of intoxication.
One can only speculate as to what took place between the time she changed buses in Saskatoon and the time she was discovered lying dead on the highway just west of Saskatoon. The sad fact is that she is dead and this is difficult for her parents and relatives to accept, but the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development contributed to her death as the result of a number of things. First, by not making specific arrangements for her transportation home, even though they had been requested to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted very briefly to lay the groundwork of the circumstances in order to point out the urgency and the terribleness of the situation as a matter of urgency of debate, because of the very things which the department of Indian affairs in its indifference and casual approach to this matter did not do and should have done. This is symptomatic of a whole, general sort of lack of sincere interest of many groups in society, including the government. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I refrained from adding the cliche "just" in front of the word "society".
There are dozens and dozens of similar cases where such indifference exists toward the fundamental human rights that we expect for ourselves but fail to accord to the native Indian people of this nation. Because the case is symptomatic of something general and is reflective of many, many other instances, I suggest this is the only opportunity that will exist for some time in the future, if the announcements of government business mean anything to us, when we will have an opportunity to discuss this matter and go into a great deal more detail with respect to the

involvement of the Indian affairs branch and the government in regard to this question.
If I could just sum up the matter of urgency, Mr. Speaker, I would say we are approaching that time of year when Christian generosity is uppermost in our minds, and no finer opportunity exists than for parliament to now take this question under advisement and discuss the humane values in our society and government attitude toward them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY IN DEATH OF GIRL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Having heard the hon. member, I am in full agreement that he may have a very legitimate grievance. The hon. member for Skeena has made the suggestion that the house should consider things which the department should have done and did not do. The hon. member says there is a grievance in this regard, and he may be quite right. But I would not think this is sufficient ground to adjourn the debates of the house for the purpose of considering the matter at this time. I can only hope, with the hon. member, that there will be an occasion at an early date when this matter might be raised again for consideration and debate by all hon. members.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder what more the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) wants. For years the cry has gone out through the land that without majority government action is impossible. Now the Prime Minister has his majority. I do not propose to question some of the methods used by his party to get it, but the point is that the minority status argument can no longer be trotted out as a convenient excuse for failure to respond to some of the pressing social issues of the day.
What more, I ask, does the Prime Minister want? Mr. Speaker, times change. How revealing it would have been if the proposal contained in 16-A for closure in advance had been made at the time when the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) were crusading essayists and editorial writers. To use the phrase of Dr. Eugene Forsey, these two gentlemen would have "torn the purple from the clouds" if such a proposal had been made in those good, halcyon days when human rights and liberties were catechism to them instead of the catchwords this plan makes them now.
We have had ample warning, though, if we had but heeded it. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) gave us a little evidence the other day. He gave us a sample of what the days ahead would be like when he talked about the throughput of the St. Lawrence Seaway. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) will become the new minister of throughput. He will be the chief programmer for the government. Under this proposal the royal prerogative will settle on a new prince, the Prime Minister. Ancient despots, if they watch us from their present stations, should envy the power of this man. One-time admirers should question his abdication of the principles which motivated his earlier and crusading days.
We seek efficiency, not impotence. We need to generate vital change. We need to speak and legislate when the speaking is done. Radical urgencies of the young, the poor, the Indians, about whom we heard just a few minutes ago, crowd upon us. But technology is not enough, as we have been compellingly reminded in a new book called "The Revolution Of Hope: Toward A Humanized Technology" by Erich Fromm. A reviewer reminds us that "For him that is joined to all the living there is hope." For any of you who do
Motion for Concurrence in Report not recognize it, that is an epigram from Ecclesiastes.
The alternatives that face man in these apocalyptic times lead either to a mechanized society in which man is caught like a helpless cog, or to a renaissance of humanism and hope, a society that puts technique not first but second, as a servant of human well-being. The absence of this philosophy in the government's proposal is what disturbs me most and troubles me deeply because of its illiberalism. It makes me wonder not about the mystery, because they are bound by this strange out of date doctrine of be-all and end-all solidarity, but why the Liberal backbenchers are saying th pv are ready to support thsss illiberal proposals.
Perhaps the most ominous development, as Dr. Fromm puts it, is that we seem to have lost control over our system and are being carried at an accelerating pace toward destruction. How did it happen? How at the very conquest of nature did man become the captive of his own creation? Fromm's answer is the same one that Emerson gave over a century ago: "Things are in the saddle, and ride mankind." Fromm puts it this way:
In the one-sided emphasis on technique and material consumption, man lost touch with himself, with life.
In a review of this book Ashley Montagu says:
People are constantly asking what they can do-
And all hon. members have responded to this frustrated cry. We heard it eloquently put just the other day in the frustration of the hon. member-I apologize to him-from Toronto, who asked about the response of the government to the problem faced by certain Polish seamen. We heard it a few minutes ago when this parliament, the agencies of parliament and the great departments of government are so unresponsive that they cannot deal with a girl leaving jail and needing transport to her home.
These frustrations and the lack of responses are the reason that all over the western world parliaments and the institutions that go with parliament are under question. And I think this is healthy. The debate is healthy if we see some resiliency in the government and particularly some flexibility.
People are constantly asking what they can do, meaning that they can in fact do nothing. That psychosis is much worse than the apathy, the passivity, on which Fromm comments so ably, for it represents not a negative uninvolvement but a positive disengagement from the human situation.
December 16. 1968

Motion for Concurrence in Report
This institution has been disengaged from the human situation for so long and instead has been dealing with its little petty problems. I will not go into them because the memory of them makes me want to be sick. But it is this disengagement that is the problem, not whether the government house leader is going to follow this new magical formula that he has proposed when he meets with himself in his office to program the business. Parliament and its members must be agents or catalysts to end this deadening passivity.
I am going to share with the house a verse by a contemporary New Brunswick poet, Alden Nowlan. In a book called "Bread, Wine and Salt" he has a poem entitled "The Nation's Capital." It is so apt it makes me shudder.
The first thing you learn here
is that the country
bears the same relationship
to the government
that outer space
bears to the earth
He goes on to depict a member of parliament having a maritini in the Chateau Laurier:
He must measure his sips and time them perfectly or there will he couriers from the Hill:
"The government may fall."
Ah, Mackenzie King,
I think I understand you:
how easy to commune with the dead
in a city wholly divorced from reality.
How easy for that former prime minister to commune from a parliament so out of touch with reality! If we need any other witnesses we have them. Jacques Maritain, the great and modern Catholic philosopher, whote a book called "Man And The State." In it he tried to re-establish the principles of democracy in a modem context. He bespeaks a redefining of the very essence of the democratic idea. He writes:
Democracy can be awkward, clumsy, defective, open to the risk of betraying itself by yielding to instincts of cowardice, or of oppressive violence-
But he goes on:
Yet the strength itself of a democratic body politic supposes justice, because it uses human energies as energies of free men, not of slaves. Nay more: a supreme effort of all the energies of freedom, in their own spiritual realm, is needed to compensate for the momentary increase in physical strength that is given Machiavellian powers by their determination to use any means whatsoever.
[Mr. Fairweather.l
I doubt that he had met the President of the Privy Council when he wrote those words. And such a supreme effort cannot arise if the body politic ignores moral values and standards. In reality strength is supremely strong only if not strength but justice is the supreme standard.
To try to reduce democracy to technology would be to try to deprive it of its very blood.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The proposed rule change in 16-A is illiberal. It is disheartening to see it stamped with the imprimatur of those who profess to be Liberals. It is unnecessary because the twenty-eighth parliament, if I am any judge of its mood, is one of co-operation and reasonableness.
In the speeches until now several large red herrings have been drawn across this motion. One red herring was that the various bills to assist farmers occupied too much of the time of the house. However, if anyone wanted to take the trouble to analyse the problem he would see that the three bills were expected to carry too much of the load in responding to the frustration of western Canada farmers because of a wet summer and a damp wheat crop. Those who do not believe me should reread the reports of those debates. The three farm bills were not particularly in question, although the high cost of money obviously was a matter of concern. It was more the fact that these bills gave some hon. members an opportunity to be representative. Once in a while we are representative, and those debates were representative in all their manifestations just as the debate was representative on the day that hon. members from Newfoundland in their representative capacity took a few hours of the time of the house to discuss a matter which to them was of very serious importance. Parliament must wait for this. The computer does not wait for it. Nor does the programmer in the Confederation building. If the computer is putting out at its full capacity it does not wait for the Newfoundland Bullet nor for wet wheat, but we make parliament wait for these things because we are here partly as representatives.
Another aspect, of course, is one that I think we must agree the Prime Minister carries out with very great effect. I refer to the educative role. The unhappy part about it is that he does most of his educating elsewhere. But we also have an educative role. That is the reason it is important that the President of the Privy Council does not spend all his
December 16, 1968

time pressing buttons in respect of his programming because education sometimes takes a little time.
The proposal of the procedure committee to abolish the committee of supply I suggest will, for various reasons, cause trouble. The principle reason, of course, is that the standing committees themselves are in no way equipped to deal with the business that will come before them. Let us not fool ourselves about this. This has been seen very clearly in respect of the British experience. The British did this a couple of years ago.
We had a Couchiching conference on the reform of parliament. Mr. Richard Crossman attended that conference. If you hear people who are in the opposition speak about this, and I suppose I obviously fall into that category, it is wonderful what they say they will do when they are in office. Mr. Crossman was a prime example. He said that the rules and proceedings of the British house would undergo such a fundamental change when he took office that one would not know the place. Well they abolished committee of supply and they are now in deep trouble in Great Britain. Mr. Stephen Fay, as reported in the Montreal Star of Saturday December 14, 1968, says:
The most radical of the changes introduced by Crossman (and one uses radical in a relative sense relating only to what happened before in parliament, not to general social change) was to take the major part of the debate on the finance bill off the floor of the House, and have the timeconsuming committee stage heard by a committee of 50 members, instead of a committee of the whole of the House of Commons. The finance bill's committee stage took five weeks of the House of Commons' time when its time was growing scarcer.
The object of the reform was to allow the house to debate more topics, and this year it did. But so great was the pressure on parliament created by new legislation, improvements were marginal. Now the Conservative party is demanding that the committee stage of the finance bill be returned to the floor of the House of Commons. The fact is that the proceedings of the small finance bill committee went virtually unreported.

Mr. Speaker, following my election to this house on June 25 of this year and after observing the proceedings as an interested private member since the opening of this session of parliament, I have a few ideas about what I feel is the function of parliament, the function of the executive in this parliament, and the relationship of the one to the other. I believe, as has been stated by many hon. members on both sides of the house, that this is one of the most important revisions of the rules to take place for many decades and perhaps the most far-reaching since the formation of this institution.
Much has been said in the country at large about parliament not functioning properly. It has been said that debates are slow, that parliament does not work quickly and efficiently and that it puts the executive, that is, the Prime Minister and his cabinet, at a great disadvantage in carrying out the governing processes in our highly technical society. Much has been made of the need for the reform of parliament by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair). He said that the mother of parliaments at Westminster had instituted far-reaching reforms that had improved their parliamentary procedure.
One of the arguments advanced by those who favour a drastic revision of our parliamentary system is that we have enormous problems of health and welfare, of housing, education, big business, big unions, and the estrangement of the common person from the governing process, of the loss of individuality by citizens and of the overpowering of his personality by the sheer complexity of government. If parliament is to blame for the state of the nation at present, as many of its critics believe and state, I do not feel that the main reform of parliament along the lines suggested by the government will in its totality materially change our economic and social situation. Indeed, a look at the state of the economic and social structure of the United Kingdom would seemingly not disclose that
3984	COMMONS
Motion jor Concurrence in Report the great changes in their parliamentary system, as proposed by many here, have materially improved their economy or that their social system has materially benefited from the parliamentary changes at Westminister.
I suggest that perhaps parliament has been much too efficient in grinding out legislation which has affected and changed the lives of our citizens and the social structure in which we live. Anyone who examines what parliament has produced for the Canadian citizen in the last 25 years cannot deny that there has been a vast amount of legislation passed which regulates, changes and affects the everyday life of the average Canadian to a degree not even thought of 50 years ago. The average Canadian has become so dependent on the government that he looks to it to provide him with sustenance in his old age, protection for his health, access to hospital facilities of a highly complex nature at no cost to himself, to provide education for his family, at least to the end of the secondary level and for much of the post-secondary level, to provide him with maintenance during periods of unemployment, and to provide him with some sort of basic maintenance throughout his whole life from womb to tomb.
The governments at all levels are spending almost 40 per cent of the national income. It is small wonder then that disruptions arise and the individual feels that the government is not doing enough for him.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
But man is nothing if he is not an individual, and no system can be devised that will make him completely happy and allow him to fit into the social slot. He has not evolved yet to the stage where any one institution or set of institutions will make him completely happy or contented. All institutions devised for government are necessarily imperfect; but I believe that the guiding principle is that institutions that are imperfect but flexible are much better than institutions that are perfect but inflexible. Institutions devised only for the government of the day, by being made more rigid and inflexible, can more easily carry on the business of the day, but they quickly become outmoded and unworkable. As a result intolerable situations develop and social frustration and eventually upheaval are the main results. So I believe that parliament must be changed, but changed always with the view in mind that the governing of man is a very imperfect process, and that we

I am not qualified at this stage to judge the effect of all of the rule changes. I would like, however, to put forward some ideas on certain of the proposed changes that I feel will not work to the best advantage of the house and of the country.
The first of these changes relates to the committee of supply. If all estimates are sent to the standing committees I feel that this will be a very retrograde step. Since coming to this house I have attempted to attend every committee of which I was a member and to carry on a reasoned questioning of the witnesses. I feel I had a considerable knowledge of much of the subject matter discussed in the committees and in the subject matters of one or two of the committees I had a high degree of technical knowledge. None the less I felt that I accomplished little and that the committees little fulfilled the function for which they were set up.
The first and most marked observation about standing committees is that the government must necessarily appoint the chairmen. In the committees I attended the chairmen were usually reasonable and attempted to give an impartial right to each member. But they certainly were under no obligation to do this and in occasional committee meetings sometimes the whole period would go by without a single opposition member being allowed to ask a question. The standing committees very much lack the impartiality and protection that the Speaker gives to the House of Commons.
It is obvious that the chairman and members of the committee from the government side would in times of scandal, mismanagement or what have you, as best they can and in their own interests make the very best effort to prevent discussion of matters that were inimicable to the government's interest. As well as that, questioning of witnesses, who are usually government employees, reveals that they will answer only as long as the government is not embarrassed.
I do not see how the new rules can make any more time available for the scrutiny of the estimates. In fact, only a very few estimates can even be given casual scrutiny. Members of parliament lack the background information intelligently to question most of the items that come before the committees.

The purpose of parliament, I am sure, is not to decide whether a project is being carried out effectively, or whether money should be spent on one portion of a project or another. This decision is much too technical, and even with the greatest back-up staff only a few, if any, members of parliament can make a meaningful contribution.
The purpose of parliament, it seems to me, is to debate whether or not a project should be carried on for a particular reason. A case in point is the abandonment of the ING project while the Post Office Department went ahead with the satellite program. It seems to me, if scientific programs are to be properly discussed, that this discussion cannot take place in a standing committee. Such a committee would be a rubberstamp for the government because all discussion could be effectively controlled by the government. The only place where a useful and realistic debate on matters of supply can be carried on in parliament is in the House of Commons. I realize that the estimates of every department cannot be scrutinized in this way because this would be too time consuming and probably unnecessary for the vast majority of departments. More and more the government of Canada is becoming involved in the taking of money from one individual and the giving of it to another. More and more the economic health of this country is dependent upon the monetary policies of the government. If the House of Commons loses control of the pursestrings and its means of criticizing and giving wide publicity to the country's monetary problems, then most legislation will be of little value.

Motion for Concurrence in Report think all of those who have taken part in the debates of this house have been earnestly trying to further the interest both of the debate and of the nation as a whole.
It does not surprise me too much that the rules of this house and the manner in which the house discharges its business should come under discussion at this time because we are entering a new era of communications and technology. People may very well feel that this demands new approaches because it is putting new stresses on those who make decisions and on the institutions which make decisions. This is just as true of the city council of Saskatoon or the town council of Biggar or the rural, municipal councils in the area where I live as it is of this house. These government bodies are being asked to spend more money and to do more things. They are being asked to undertake a greater role in the everyday affairs of individual men.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
There was a time in the area where I live when, to fix a road, someone took what we call a slip scraper and filled in the hole in the road. That is all there was to it and that was sufficient to repair the road. Now no one would think of doing that. The ordinary, individual taxpayer has nothing to do with it. Certain moneys are voted, certain taxes are raised, council decides where a road is to be and it is built there. The situation has completely changed in less than most men's lifetime.
Now we have new means of communication. Television is beamed across this continent, across all the civilized world, telling people what a glorious era they live in and how lovely it is to belong to the United States or Canadian middle class for those who can afford to enjoy its benefits. Television programs tell us almost everyone can own a motor car, almost everyone can get a loan for more horses-I forget the exact wording of the advertising. In this new era of technology and communication the real problem facing parliament and the people of Canada is the difficulty of communicating between the ordinary citizen of Canada and those who decide many of the things that affect his life.
In some ways it is more difficult to communicate now than it was in the days of the slip scraper. In those days of the past when your road had to be fixed a councillor would come to you and say, "Well, Joe, take your horses and fix the road." Both men knew what they were talking about. They knew what had to be done, knew it was essential because they


could see the hole in the road, and as a result the job was done. It is different now. By one means or another we must convince the individual in Moncton, New Brunswick, in the Gaspe peninsula, in the prairies or out on the west coast that what is done in this parliament is essential for the individual and, more than that, that it is in his interest. These proposed rule changes are so important because, as I understand them, they will alter the ability to communicate.
If you limit the right of an opposition member or backbencher in this house to express the wishes and opinions of the people who sent him here, you limit or change any communications that might take place between him and his constituents. If he does not have the opportunity to stand up in this house and speak, then to a degree you limit his right to communicate. If he is not reported as having expressed in this house the wishes and opinions of the people he represents, most people in his constituency will say ultimately, "Oh, that individual-we should never have elected him." If they then send another man and the same thing happens, they will ultimately conclude that there is really no point in sending anybody. When we get to that point parliament will really have become downgraded. Parliament in my opinion will not be downgraded by excess of debate but rather by paucity of debate, by the inability of those who have been sent here to express effectively the needs of those who sent them. This is what we should be concerned about.
There has been discussion here about tradition, particularly the tradition of that parliament from which we have drawn our ideas and on which we have patterned much of our procedure. There has been discussion about rules and about the manner in which members carry out their roles in the mother of parliaments as well as about the manner in which debate is controlled there. Traditionally the individual member has the right to say what he thinks in the mother of parliaments and the right to a forum where he can say it. In short, he has the right to express his point of view. That is the basis of any real parliamentary tradition. It took centuries for those rights and traditions to be achieved. It took a long time for individual members to have the right to say in an appropriate forum what they thought, without fear or favour-and that is important because we must have certain guarantees in our parliaments. It took a struggle to achieve our rights and traditions, and it was not easy. We glory in the background of the British parliament, but I point
December 16, 1988	COMMONS
out that it was not always as it now is. Only in 1929, if my memory serves me correctly, did universal sufferage become general in the United Kingdom. That is not long ago. Our democratic institutions really are not that old and we have not used them for long-for a few generations only.
When we discuss rules in this house the most important question we ought to ask ourselves is not whether our time is well spent or otherwise but whether the rights of individual members of parliament are being preserved. Are we preserving the right of parliament to act effectively on the needs of the times? Are we preserving its right to act effectively through the media of publicity- press, radio and television-so that there is a two-way communication between hon. members and those who sent them? In regard to this chamber itself the real question is not whether the present procedure wastes time but whether it serves the people. That is a positive question. If the answer to that question is yes, then this parliament and this house are serving their purpose. There will be no communication through the press or by radio or television unless this parliament plays its part. Certainly there will be communication by the executive arm of the government. From time to time the representatives of the press will ask ministers what they are doing and ministers will give reports over television or radio. What the country wants to know is what individual members are doing.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Mention has been made of additional work being undertaken by the standing committees. This may be a practical way of taking some of the load off the house. In the short time I have been here I have served on two committees-continuously on one of them. We held 11 meetings and the minister concerned attended four of them. I would say the chairman did a fair and even-handed job. But the committee was lacking in services; one could wait for days before the transcript of the proceedings had been prepared and was in members' hands. One could attend a second meeting and possibly a third before the proceedings of the first meeting were available. The steering committee met once. The chairman called it twice but only once was there a full meeting of the steering committee.
We called certain witnesses before us. They appeared and answered questions fairly. But it is likely that many more witnesses would have been necessary, and a great deal more
DEBATES	3987
Motion for Concurrence in Report time, before a complete picture of all the activities of the departments concerned could have been presented. I seriously question whether committees can effectively do the work which has been done in the house. This chamber does provide a forum for debate; it does provide for questions to be asked and answered. More important still, it provides an opportunity for an individual member to state his position. This house is the only real forum available to an hon. member. The only real protection against big government is parliament. This is the place where the representatives of the people can speak without fear or favour.
Whether we like it or not-and I suppose some people do not like it-government is playing an increasing role in the economic and political affairs of this nation. This trend is more likely to increase than to decrease. The choice is not, as was suggested today, between helping farmers to sell wheat and taking over their farms, placing them in the position of hired men. It is suggested that the government must either own the land and hire the farmer to produce or step outside the picture altogether. These are not the alternatives we face in this country. This idea is archaic. It is as out of date as the man with two horses pulling a slip scraper.
In this country we quit arguing about the alternatives of capitalism and communism years ago. The issue is not even relevant any more. The question we face really involves the degree and the manner in which government, business, industry and labour are to be mixed-how they will live together and under what conditions, the degree to which government will enter into the economic affairs of the nation. This is why parliament is of prime importance. It is parliament, either by positive decisions or by negative decisions, which will effectively direct the affairs of this nation or opt cut. It is therefore essential that parliament be a powerful force in our affairs, and for this reason we should not leave power in the hands of big government without seeing to it that the balancing effect of members who sit on the back benches is preserved.
The degree of government intervention can be observed day after day. There was a picture in the press the other day of the Minister of Labour just after he had successfully resolved the Air Canada dispute.

I agree with you, sir. But consider the implications. Air Canada is owned by Canada and controlled by the government of the day. The individual who moved to settle this dispute with a powerful union was a minister of the crown answerable to this house. In these circumstances, how important it is that members of parliament should be able to ask that minister: how well did you perform this service and how fairly did you perform it vis-a-vis the labour union? As I see it, this trend toward government influence and intervention is likely to accelerate rather than diminish.
Let me give hon. members another example, this time from the Globe and Mail of December 6. Here is a report saying that the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company of Winnipeg expects to complete its $18.4 million takeover of Sylvite of Canada Limited, Regina, by Monday. I would direct attention particularly to one paragraph of this report:
Development at the mine has so far cost more than 10 million. Mr. Austin said it is two years from production. He said pre-production expenses for the Sylvite project will be used to reduce Hudson Bay's taxable income beginning this year; without this provision for tax relief, the take-over would not have been undertaken.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Government, by its taxing policies, is the arbitrator, the decider whether or not a business take-over occurs, whether or not a certain project continues. In that light we see the importance of parliament in this debate.
I think it is also relevant to this procedural issue to ask ourselves why the government wishes rule 16-A. Why do the men who sit on the other side of the house wish unlimited power? To make these kinds of decisions so they can take action, or possibly so they do not have to take action? Which is it? Is it so that the government can deal with rising unemployment or so it will not have to deal with it? Is it so that it may deal with the situation fast developing in western Canada with respect to grain, or so it may be avoided? Is it so that debate will not be quite so severe, so prolonged, and so that not as much can be said about it? Is it so that someone may deal with the groundflshery situation on the east coast, or so that it can be avoided?
To what end are these powers sought? So that the government can do things or so that action can be avoided? So that the government can deal with the vast technological changes, so that the political and economic climate of Canada can be kept abreast of

these changes, or so that action can be avoided and leave the people of Canada individually to struggle along by themselves?
I suppose there are some people who support this move, but I submit that no prime minister who conceives of parliament as the dominant force of Canadian political and economic life can support this kind of proposal to parliament and to the Canadian people. Some portions of the press are becoming concerned. I read this editorial from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of last week:
A government that is unconcerned about the privileges and responsibilities of its opposition deserves a chance to serve in opposition for a while.
The Liberal government in Ottawa may be demonstrating such unconcern in its proposed rule changes for the House of Commons. One of the changes would give it the power to set limits on opposition members' debating time.
It goes on to say:
-an opposition in Parliament performs a vital function in a democracy-a function which could be significantly hampered by the proposed rule.
Normally government policy undergoes fairly thorough scrutiny in caucus before it is presented to the house. This can have a tempering effect on questionable proposals, but it is not a substitute for public examination by an opposition that is not interested in furthering the political ends of the government-
If the government is truly unconcerned about this, Canadians would have good reason to consider giving the Liberals another term or two in opposition-as a reminder that an opposition's role in parliament is sometimes of importance equal to that of the government.
Some of the press and some people outside the house are concerned about what is being proposed here. What the government seeks by these procedural changes is the impotence of parliament. Once the executive arm of the government has achieved its objective and deprived the opposition parties of the ability and freedom to protest, then it has automatically done the same to its own backbenchers. It can follow a course of political inactivity in an economic sense. It will then be able to follow the United States tradition of withdrawing progressively from small islands of economic intervention and it will not move to take effective economic action.
This is one of the differences between the tradition of our system and that of the American system. Since 1867 our parliament has been a parliament of action. It took the action necessary to weld Canada together. It created the transportation system that would
December 16, 1968	COMMONS
do that. It created Air Canada because Canada has to be welded together with a communications system. It created the C.B.C. You find none of these important means of communication in our neighbour to the south. Our neighbour to the south took a course whereby congress was not active. We, for our part, have taken the course of saying that in certain fields, at certain times, in certain necessities, we would be active.
One of the saddest things I have ever observed on television was the poor people's march on Washington, to see them in their thousands sit outside congress and yet congress took no action. Why? Because this is not their tradition. This is the same thing as the farmers selling their own wheat. The government is not concerned. Unless we turn things around, unless we reverse the traditions and the courses we have followed in the past we will continue to say that government plays a role in the economic affairs of Canada, in the planning, in the working out of our long and short-term objectives, in deciding the course of destiny for the Canadian people. If we follow our traditions this we will say and this we will do.
Our tradition has been one of communication and also of participation, not only in this house but on the local level. In the area I come from it does not matter whether people's antecedents were Ukrainians, Czechoslovakians or Germans. They were expected to and did take part in the day to day affairs of the councils and other government bodies in that area and in that province. This is the real tradition of Canada, not a tradition of race or of any particular ethnic origin but a tradition of people working together to achieve the end which they think is desirable, not being negative or afraid but being positive and constructive and willing to strike out on new paths when it was necessary to achieve those objectives which they desired. The rule changes proposed here negate the traditional approach which we have created in the short time we have been a nation.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I am not dedicated to the preservation of any "ism" because the isms often lead us into trouble. But I am dedicated to the preservation of the life and vitality of this parliament and to seeing it as an instrument to further the interest and welfare of the Canadian people. I believe the people of Saskatoon-Biggar see it that way. They expect us to act. They do not expect us simply to keep the ring, as someone described the British parliament in
DEBATES	3989
Motion for Concurrence in Report its heyday of Conservativism, but to keep safe the economic interests of the country.
We are being asked to limit the participation of individuals in this parliament while at the same time the government sets up regional desks some place back in the hinterland to give them advice when they should be seeking advice from their own backbenchers and the members of the opposition, if only they would listen. "Regional desk" is a good term. It is a nice term-a desk made of steel or wood which does not talk to anybody. It is the people who will sit behind the desks who will do the talking. If they are anything like most political servitors they will tell you, when you get their answers, all the things you want to hear. If you want the truth, then you should listen to those who do not agree with you and not to those who are committed to agree with you beforehand.
As is the case in respect of those who have spoken before me today, I am completely and utterly opposed to the provisions of 16A. They will muzzle and limit this parliament and it will be that much less effective if the government has its way.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that this is one point of order that is in order. I wish to thank hon. members for their very kind wishes. I think the wind has been taken out of my sails a little, but I am sure I will recover. First of all I should like to congratulate the members of the committee on procedure who, but for the grace of God, did an excellent job in their efforts. I should like to congratulate my colleagues who worked on that committee. I have come to know my colleagues in this regard. As a new member I was impressed by their sincerity and the role
3990	COMMONS
Motion for Concurrence in Report they took in trying to bring about changes in the rules that would benefit the whole house and the whole nation because parliament does serve the whole nation of Canada. I wonder why such a stipulation as 16-A was ever brought in as part of the report. I notice the attempt of the government house leader to apologize for its existence on Friday when he did the sort of thing one would do for a youngster who complains, that is, give him a popsicie or a candy. I have wondered what the motive was behind 16-A. After having listened attentively to a number of eminent members of this house make their representations I realize that 16-A was included deliberately to give to the government the power this provision gives.
Having read during my days as a student a number of eminent writers of the 17th century and their criticism of the British judicial system I was reminded of a statement attributed, I believe, to Pope when he said that beggars hang that jury men may dine. This is a very succinct summation of some of the inequities of the judicial system of Britain a few centuries ago. I wonder whether this is not a complete summation also of the content of 16A in that we will hang because they are hungry. This is the attitude of the government toward the problems which exist in this nation.
I certainly do not intend to stand here and take issue with many of the reforms that have been recommended in the report of the special committee on procedure. X am one new member of parliament who is a little impatient and who, like all new backbenchers of all parties, would like to see the government in power take action on many of the social, economic and other problems of our nation. I can say I have been very impatient with the way in which this government to date has not faced up to the problems confronting this nation, despite its great majority.
If I were to make one point only in my few remaining remarks I would dwell heavily on the one point which caught my attention in the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) last Tuesday. I shall quote from the remarks of the hon. gentleman as they appear at page 3758 of Hansard. These remarks represent the feelings of our leader and of all hon. members in this house who are legitimately and sincerely interested in the regional problems of Canada. They represent in a very brief fashion the part that parliament must play in dealing with these

DEBATES	December 16, 1968
regional problems. The Leader of the Opposition said:
X suggest we must remember that this is the only national forum in which spokesmen for all parts of Canada can speak and expect to be heard. I need not remind the house that different regions of the country have specific problems and points of view. Discussion in a national forum helps to knit the regions into a whole nation and to build a stronger unity. It seems likely that one of the serious casualties of any major limitation upon the time of debate would be the right of spokesmen to be adequately heard on the problems of the regions. I suggest that national unity would suffer.
As a member of a particular region of Canada I feel, as I assume all members who represent particular regions of Canada feel, that any attempt to restrict legitimate debate on matters pertaining to regional problems would be an infringement of the rights of the people of the various parts of Canada and the people in all of Canada. I consider that one of my main tasks as a new member, and one of the main tasks of any member of parliament, is to sensitize the members of the government in respect of the various regions of Canada, because regardless of how competent, capable or sincere a minister is he cannot expect to understand fully the importance of the particular problems which relate to the various regions. I suspect that had these ministers been so sensitized they would have made an effort to sensitize the bureaucracy into putting the policies and programs of the government into effect.
I consider that the regional problems of Canada which face the whole nation right across the dominion must be brought to the attention of parliament as time progresses and especially because of the changes in government and the changes of ministers of the government who occupy different roles and new portfolios. These people have to be sensitized to our problems across the dominion. How are the ministers and the government going to understand what is going on in Canada if we are not allowed and permitted the right to debate these issues in this house? I am amazed at the attitude of some of the new members who have suggested that by bringing in the proposed 16-A or anything which will or can be intended for the purpose of eliminating debate in the House of Commons they will be better off.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Perhaps I might be permitted to refer to my own problems for a moment. I have had the opportunity since I came to the house of mentioning several problems peculiar to the Atlantic region and I shall continue to do so
December 16, 1968

if the Speaker permits me and with the good will of the house. This is only one region of Canada which has and will continue to have social and economic problems so long as the government continues to take its present attitude. A number of members from the Atlantic region have debated the function change of the C.N.R. These remarks were made during our discussion of the C.N.R. financing bill. I only regret that we did not call for a vote and refuse to provide the financing sought. Any body such as the C.T.C. or the C.N.R. which proceeds to act as dictatorially and inconsiderately as they have acted does not deserve the support of this representative assembly.
I suggest that if there had been members of parliament from the Atlantic region who had been prepared to stand in this house during the last parliament to indicate the importance of a railway system to one province of Canada, Newfoundland, the Canadian Transport Commission and the C.N.R. would not have dared to make the kind of decision they have now made so far as our railway system is concerned. Had we had members with the gumption to get up in this house and make the points we have now made we would not be faced with this very serious problem.
We have heard members from British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Quebec and Newfoundland talk at length since this parliament commenced about the serious problems facing our fishing industry. We have had little difficulty in convincing our own colleagues of the seriousness of the state of that particular economic aspect of the Canadian way of life, but we have had great difficulty in obtaining the interest of the minister in respect of our problems. Unless we are permitted to stand here and present our cases, and if the minister continues to take no heed of what we are saying, we will find the whole Canadian nation in a much more serious economic state of affairs than exists even now.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does not understand the problem facing that industry. Undoubtedly he has heard some talk about it and he may have heard some ministers refer to it, but neither he nor the hon. member for Rosedale is familiar with the Atlantic fishery and perhaps they are not too interested. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) and his colleagues might well be sincerely interested in this problem, but they are obviously not fully aware of the serious circumstances involved.
Motion for Concurrence in Report What I am trying to say is that unless members of parliament are permitted the right to stand here and indicate to the house and the rest of the people of Canada those problems which exist, the government may never do anything. When one speaks in this house one can influence policy because of press coverage, and one can sensitize the whole nation to the problems of various regions. Perhaps this right will also be taken away shortly. I hope for the sake of the members of the press gallery that they will still be in existence in the new year, and that the Prime Minister does not remove them as a Christmas present to some of his hon. friends.
Unfortunately I was not here on Friday afternoon to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Bruce. I should like to have been present because I was amazed at what he said about this institution being the most exclusive club in Canada. He used that phrase frequently throughout his remarks, and he suggested we should be ashamed of ourselves because we have only passed eight or ten pieces of legislation. Although he did not use this phrase, he said in so many words that parliament should become a sausage factory. This phrase has been used in respect of some educational systems in Canada which turn out young people as though through a sausage factory. That hon. member also said we should be ashamed of ourselves for asking the silly questions we pose in the house. I believe the only reason for this attitude is that a number of Liberal backbenchers are frustrated because they came here with the great idea of taking part in debate and with great ideas about our democratic system of government but have since found different.
Many Liberal backbenchers are blessed with ability and would love to get in their two cents worth but are not permitted to do so, not only because the government house leader and others steal the show most of the time but also because time does not permit. This might be one of the problems. In any event, quite a number of Liberal backbenchers are really frustrated, and I have talked with a number of them. They feel-I was going to say taken in or sucked in but that is not very parliamentary-they have been sold a bill of goods and that these reforms will result in giving them greater flexibility in being able to take part and put their points across.
One point which has been made is that the committees will become the forum for debate. Consequently this has given a number of
3992	COMMONS
Motion for Concurrence in Report Liberal backbenchers the feeling that, goodness gracious, there will be a chance for them to get into the debate. They feel they have lots of ability having spent ten years in this or that legislature, or having been mayor of a great metropolitan area, or this or that or something else. They feel that if they can get on a committee which is to be a forum for debate they will be able to get their points across and make a contribution.
I am really shocked by this feeling on the part of the Liberal backbenchers because they ought to realize that the house leader who controls parliament also controls the committees. We had an example of this last week when one committee functioned well and brought in a motion. This motion did not meet with the approval of the house leader and he threw it out. He can decide what is to happen in a committee and who will take part in the debate, when a resolution will be brought in and when it will be debated. He can decide pretty well whether committees will exist. I am shocked by those frustrated Liberal backbenchers who feel that by limiting the debate in this house they will have a greater opportunity to talk about their own constituency problems. They seem to feel that by limiting debate as a result of the proposed rule 16A they will get rid of their frustrations.

One of our major problems in this 20th century is in realizing the fact that we are living in a changing society. As Aristotle said when he was a growing boy, society is always changing. There is a need to make decisions which are going to result in a sensitive approach to the needs of people. This is one of the greatest challenges which faces any organization or institution. I am surprised that any Liberal backbencher could support the proposed change in 16A when in actual fact all they are doing is relinquishing their right to speak. Under the proposed 16A no one will have the right to speak except the Prime Minister, two or three of his friends in the front row and perhaps two or three of my friends in our front row. The opportunity for a backbencher to speak will be completely eliminated. We might as well go home. Liberal backbenchers might as well realize this, go home and send other stuffed shirts to Ottawa, or perhaps a tape recorder, because they will have nothing to do.
No one denies that we need changes in parliament. Having followed the proposed

changes since I have been here as a new member, and the report brought forward by the special committee, I believe the committee has done an excellent job in coping with some of the changes which were needed.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I think we need a change, for example, in the sensitivity of the bureaucracy in Ottawa to the needs of the people. We need a change in the efficiency with which decisions of parliament are carried out by the bureaucracy, which tends to bog down and because of its inefficiency, rules, regulations and inadequacy never really puts into effect many of the decisions made by parliament. We need a change in the attitude of ministers of the crown in answering questions in the house. A Liberal backbencher told me that he made a count and one question, the same question, has been asked 40 times since the beginning of the session. He thought this was a terrible reflection on the opposition. What is the minister or his department doing if the question has to be asked 40 times? Obviously an answer has not been given to the question.
I have been frustrated to the point where Mr. Speaker must have taken great exception to my presence here, and rightfully so, as a member of parliament standing and asking questions and receiving nothing more than a shrug of the shoulders for an answer or a "ditto" here, a "ditto" there, here a "ditto", there a "ditto", everywhere a "ditto". I have been really frustrated, especially on occasions such as today when we have a chronic emergency developing in one of our provinces and have not been able to get the ministers concerned into the house to answer questions. We need a change in the attitude of the government toward taxation. I listened with great interest during the budget debate to a number of members, including some of the Liberals, speaking about the aims of the government. This government still retains an out of date attitude toward taxation. Apparently it has never read some of the eminent documents emanating from
December 16, 1968

great writers to the south who have been advising administrations in that country. The attitude of our government toward taxation is 18th century. I do not think the government has one bit of interest in the farmers of Canada. We need a great change by the government in its attitude toward the farmers of western Canada. I have never heard such important speeches by sincere individuals, with so little result from this government, as I have in respect of the farmers of western Canada.
We wonder, when we rise in our places as members of the house, not only of the opposition but of Canada's parliament, whether this government gives one darn about the farmers and the fishermen of Canada. We wonder about its attitude toward unemployment. I read only two or three days ago that there has been a significant increase in the unemployment rate in Canada. I think the figures for the nation indicate that 4.4 per cent of the people of Canada are now unemployed. This is an increase of some 70,000 over the number of unemployed for the same period last year. Yet still we talk about a just society. Still we talk about the amenities of modern life. This is the kind of change of attitude that we can do with right now. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that none of my colleagues would take exception to this kind of change of attitude by the government.
Sometimes I wonder, listening to some members taking part in debate, whether they really realize whose rights we are talking about. We are not talking about the rights of the Liberal government. We are not talking about the rights of the Prime Minister or those of the hon. member for Rosedale, the present house leader of the government. We are not talking about the rights of the Tories, N.D.P.'ers or Creditistes. When we speak about rights we are talking about the rights of the Canadian people.

We are being asked to make parliament responsible to the Liberal house leader. This is in actual fact what could happen if rule 16A were passed in its present form. As I say, Mr. Speaker, we would make parliament responsible to the Liberal house leader. I do not mind going along with reform. I do not mind gambling a little bit. But I am certainly not going to commit suicide.

Motion for Concurrence in Report
I ask all hon. members to tell their constituents the exact nature of proposed rule 16A. Members should tell their constituents exactly what powers it could give any house leader. They should tell their people what powers it could give to the present house leader and to those who would follow the hon. member for Rosedale. The hon. member for Rosedale may well not be in the house after the next election, but in actual fact if we passed this rule we would be giving this power to anybody who happens to be the government house leader in the future.
I ask hon. members to tell their constituents what this rule could really mean. They should ask their constituents whether they would be satisfied if their rights were relinquished. This is what is sought to be done by rule 16A. We are elected to represent constituencies and to be the voice of our people in parliament. It is not the voice of John Lundrigan from Gander-Twillingate, or some other insignificant character in history who will pass on after a few years and that will be all that is heard of him. We will not be giving up the right of this parliament but the right of the people in our constituencies who have been gracious enough to give us the right to speak on their behalf.
I ask hon. members to ask their constituents whether they are prepared to give up the right of members to speak for them on the farming industry, the fishing industry, the mining industry or the housing situation. I ask hon. members:	If the house leader
decides that he is going to eliminate debate, as indeed he can under the proposed rule, who will speak for the miners of British Columbia?
