subtopic: SUGGESTED CONSTRUCTION OF FUNDY TRAIL
SUGGESTED CONSTRUCTION OF FUNDY TRAIL
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of giving immediate consideration to the provision of special financial assistance to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia for the construction of the Fundy Trail from St. Stephen, New Brunswick to Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, using existing roads where possible, and assisting financially in connecting existing roads in order that a scenic highway be available to aid in the promotion of the tourist industry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks I should like to refer briefly to the last few words of the resolution which read as follows:
-in order that a scenic highway be available to aid in the promotion of the tourist industry.
These words represent the crux of the resolution and my purpose in bringing this motion before the house. The purpose of the resolution is to attempt to persuade the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, to take the necessary measures to develop the Fundy trail as a tourist attraction which will greatly enhance the economic position of these two provinces. What is the Fundy trail? It is nothing new. For more than 50 years imaginative people have envisioned a 550 mile specially developed highway skirting the Fundy shore from St. Stephen, New Brunswick, to Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. It would traverse some of the most breathtaking scenery on the North American continent. It would open up areas of historic significance, places where Canadian history was born such as the ancient French forts of La Tour and Beausejour; the land of Evangeline immortalized by Longfellow, and Blomidon and Tan-tramar, the land of the famous Fundy tides. These are places that have an irresistible appeal for tourists, both from Canada and the United States.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The Fundy vacation trail when completed would be 550 miles of pastoral beauty and magnificent seascape graced by dozens of locations enshrined in history, two cities, 15 towns, 350 communities and 490 miles of beaches, inlets and coves washed by the
3996	COMMONS
Construction of Fundy Trail world's highest tides. The trail will trace the entire bay of Fundy shore between St. Stephen, New Brunswick, and Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, its length halved between the two provinces. Its terminal points will be joined by two ferry services.
Developing the Fundy vacation trail means a long-term project, an immense investment and rich benefit, not least during the period of its construction, to the locales through which it will pass. To bring the trail as it now exists up to promotable standards by improving or diverting roads already built and linking them with new highways will cost Nova Scotia and New Brunswick an estimated $25 million. Viewed as a total concept, it may represent an investment of $100 million. The trail's development will inject financial adrenalin into areas in which it is much needed. It will stimulate large, localized capital expenditure. It will breed wide employment opportunity. It will give rise to commerce, particularly that associated with recreation, boat building, sports and resort development, dining and accommodation facilities. It will boost municipal coffers through additional tax revenue available from tourist accommodation services operating for a longer period of the year.
But it is the tourist boom that offers the Fundy vacation trail its most attractive potential. The influx of visitors into both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick has swelled during the last five years. The measure of the Fundy vacation trail challenge is the scope of its potential: it will be within easy reach of both American and Canadian travellers and is seen as the subject of a May to November season.
Let me again refer to the last sentence of the resolution in which I point out that this highway would basically be an aid in promoting the tourist industry. Bight now let me clear up any misconceptions that have arisen that the Fundy trail is being advocated simply as another highway for transportation purposes. This view has been put forward by New Brunswick highways minister, Andre Kichard, and on these grounds he has dismissed any immediate consideration of the project on the basis that other highway improvements are more urgent. The minister has missed the point. The Fundy trail is desirable not as just another highways system but ,as an addition to our highways system which would lead to a vast increase in tourist potential and an attraction of more dollars to the maritime economy.
.[Mr, Thomas (Moncton) .1
DEBATES	December 16, 1968
The Fredericton Daily Gleaner in an editorial in the December 3, 1968, edition had this to say:
Highways Minister Andre Richard says in a speech at Moncton that the war on poverty must take precedence over all other measures to improve the maritimes. Projects such as the New Bruns-wick-Prince Edward Island causeway, the Fundy trail, the Chignecto canal, the Corridor road across Maine, would be highly desirable, he says, when considered on an individual basis. "But considered in total, they would immediately bankrupt any society."
We agree with Mr. Richard that poverty should have top priority. Through the years we have never departed from that concept. But can poverty be cured without introducing industry? And how can industry be introduced without the implementation of projects to pave the way for it?
We disagree with Mr. Richard where he fails to distinguish between expenditure and investment. We believe that investment in certain great public works projects would yield a rich return. We believe that it would not be spending wealth, it would be creating wealth. And there is the fundamental difference in the two philosophies.
The Fundy trail would be an immense attraction to the tourist industry which could be increased if we could interest the great population to the south of us to come to this area.
This government has pledged itself to the correction of regional disparity. We are all aware of the problems of the Atlantic provinces-unemployment higher than the national average and underemployment because of lack of job opportunities. We realize the fact that we are at a great disadvantage in competing on the Canadian market because of our location and our distance from the highly populated areas. But this very handicap can become our greatest asset. Because of our very lack of industrialization and our underpopulation, this area has an irresistible appeal for the millions of people living in the heavily populated areas of Quebec, Ontario and the eastern United States. We are in the happy position of being next door neighbours to one of the biggest tourist markets on the North American continent-the state of New York and the New England states. These areas have become so congested that we are in a wonderful position to attract this tremendous tourist potential to the Fundy area.
The Fundy trail should not be confused with any express highway program. It is an opportunity for both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to join in a dynamic and further development of the tourist industry of these provinces. Tourism today is more than big business; it is a gigantic self-help program capable of producing highly lucrative returns solely in the public interest. The Fundy vacation trail would be a tourist magnet. The trail
December 16, 1968	COMMONS
would be an impetus to the employment of labour throughout the Atlantic provinces and would use locally made supplies and material. The Fundy vacation trail is the key to an improved standard of living and a better economic future for the Fundy folk and their families.
What can this mean? Tourism today is our second largest industry, second only to our forest products in bringing in foreign dollars. If it were not for these dollars from the tourist trade, our balance of payments with the United States would be in serious imbalance. In the present year some 2,800,000 people visited the province of New Brunswick alone and left behind $87 million. The tourist industry in Canada must continue to grow and remain healthy.
A recent study in the United States analysed the growth of tourism there. It concluded that increased leisure, increased incomes and increased mobility accounted for only half of the increase in tourist usage. It appears that some of the conditions of an increasingly urban life are adding to the number of North Americans who seek some part of their pleasure out of doors.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
We can look ahead and predict a 30-hour week. We can look ahead and foresee the day when no family will have an income below the poverty line. We can see the day when the mobility of man is enhanced so that a journey half way round the world is counted as a week end trip. The technical capability is almost with us. The productive genius of man is almost boundless. His social management is less to be commended. We can foresee the man of the future with an even more urgent demand for outdoor recreation facilities. The combined post-war phenomenon of more affluence and disposable leisure time has given rise to accelerated public outdoor recreational demands which have placed radically increasing pressures not only upon our national parks and outdoor recreational space but on all other landscape resources as well. The problem of providing adequate parks and recreational and other types of open space has become one of the major problems in an accelerating urban society.
The 500,000 people in the immediate area of the Fundy trail have recognized the need and expressed overwhelming support for this venture. Cities, towns, municipalities, boards of trade and the press have expressed enthusiastic approval. Let me quote one or two of
DEBATES	3997
Construction of Fundy Trail these endorsements. The first is from the Truro Daily News of June 16, 1966:
The construction of such a trail would be of great benefit to the two provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and if developed energetically and wisely will allow all communities to capitalize on what is now the area's largest industry. Such a project would not only give major impetus to the tourist industry but additional jobs would be created, as well as the possibility of the establishment of new industries.
My second reference is to the Moncton Daily Times of September 15, 1964:
The 1964 tourist season now drawing to a close has been a record breaking one in point of throngs of American and Canadian visitors ... The expansion of Fundy park is a project that cannot long be postponed, if its value and usefulness as a tourist mecca and popular outdoor rendez-vous for our own citizenry is to be maintained.
If it was urgent in 1964, Mr. Speaker, it is that much more urgent today.
Recognizing the need for such a project we may ask, how can it best be realized? I suggest that the federal government ought to take immediate steps to complete the unfinished portion of the trail between St. Martin's and Point Wolfe. The cost of this has been estimated at $12 million. Then action should be taken at once to enlarge the present Fundy national park which is the second smallest park in Canada. Lands should be acquired on the western side to develop new beaches and playgrounds and camping areas. The existing 29 trailer hook-ups are woefully inadequate to meet the increasing demand. Why, one trailer club in Moncton alone has over 100 members. Land is available at present and at small expense could be equipped with sewage facilities and trailer hook-ups which would more than double the present capacity. An excellent nine hole golf course attracts more players than can be accommodated. Plans should be made to enlarge it as soon as possible.
To complete the unfinished section of highway and to bring existing highways and bridges up to standard would require an expenditure of some $25 million. It is not for a minute suggested that this be done immediately, but I do feel that a ten-year program with a total expenditure of $25 million would bring at least another 200,000 tourists to the area. On the basis of figures now available this would bring in some $10 million of additional revenue. Surely this would be one of the best ways imaginable for us to bring living standards in the maritimes up to the level of the rest of Canada. The need for such a project has long been recognized.
December 16, 1968

Construction of Fundy Trail
Before closing may I refer to an editorial in the Moncton Daily Times of October 6, 1966, headed "Fundy Trail Should be Built". In part this is what it says:
The construction of the trail would involve an expenditure in the vicinity of $25 million and this is no mean sum. Nevertheless, the expenditure would be a worth-while investment. It would stimulate tourism, thus benefitting Canada as a nation, and it would lead to a tremendous expansion of tourist facilities in the affected parts of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The $25 million would generate many additional millions of dollars worth of building. The effects, both short-term and long-term, would spread through the areas' economy like ripples in a pond.
With every day of delay that passes the cost of the project will increase. The sound economy would be to embark upon this undertaking at an early date. Such a project would not be inflationary in this part of Canada for it is a well known fact -and the federal government has now recognized this-that the inflationary pressures which apply elsewhere in Canada are not operating here.
New Brunswick and Nova Scotia cannot shoulder the burden of building the trail themselves. Aid must be forthcoming from either the federal government or a federal agency such as the Atlantic Development Board. But the project must be tackled. Common sense demands it.

subtopic: SUGGESTED CONSTRUCTION OF FUNDY TRAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time because the matter now before the house is of considerable interest to me. The proposed Fundy trail, in order to cover the shoreline of the bay of Fundy, would naturally be partly in New Brunswick and partly in Nova Scotia, and be connected at the provincial border by the isthmus of Chignecto. As you approach the northern end of this isthmus you enter Westmorland county, part of the constituency of Westmorland-Kent that I have the honour to represent in this house. Since it is apparent that a segment of this trail would pass through part of my riding it is only natural that 1 should show interest in any undertaking, no matter how small or big, if it will contribute to the economy of my riding and province.
How many times in past years have I wished for some magic wand which would enable me to grant the many valid requests coming from all segments of our local industries-the requests of farmers for better marketing facilities and higher incomes, the requests of the fishermen, to whom one's heart really goes out when one sees their need for better docking facilities and services. It has been their lifelong dream to see these improvements accomplished. I am also thinking of transportation rates that will enable our small and few processing industries to compete with the big and far away centres. I
[Mr. Thomas (Moncton) J

also think with emphasis about our tourist industry, the future potential of which cannot be overemphasized.
Requests from these and many other areas come our way each day, and it is our duty as elected members of parliament to shoulder our responsibilities. Every hon. member, I am sure, wishes to find immediate solutions to problems and it is here, Mr. Speaker, that we face reality.
Before continuing with my remarks about New Brunswick's participation I wish to read an editorial contained in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of February 26 which gives a clear indication of the priorities established by Premier Smith and his government, the members of which show responsibility in their decision. The heading is "The Fundy Trail", and the editorial says in part:
Premier Smith is reported to have made a most significant qualification to his official support for the building of the proposed vacation trail along the Fundy coastline of Nova Scotia.
Logan Barnhill, a member of the Fundy trail committee, said last week that Premier Smith had assured the committee of the provincial government's "solid backing" for the project. At an "opportune time", Mr. Smith was reported to have told him, the Nova Scotia government would give the project its full support, including financial aid.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
"Opportune time" is surely a significant qualification. There is no doubt that the Fundy trail envisaged as a tourist highway running from the United States border along New Brunswick's Fundy coast and then westward again along the Nova Scotia coastline is a most desirable objective. At present, so much of the Fundy coastline on both sides of the bay, and so many of its beaches and small harbours, are inaccessible. Certainly on the Nova Scotia shore, the coastline often can be reached only by dirt roads. The scenic beauty of much of the area can be enjoyed only by a few patient and resolute motorists.
A Fundy trail might do for southeastern New Brunswick and the Minas basin and Annapolis valley areas of Nova Scotia what the Cabot trail has done for non-industrial Cape Breton. It would be a boon to tourism, the motel and catering industry, and to the economies of the communities along its route.
Yet today is not the appropriate time to start work on the Fundy trail. This province's trunk road system is now being transformed in several regions. New, high-speed highways are being built, at high cost, between Halifax and Truro along those portions of the trans-Canada Highway not yet modernized, between Halifax and the valley towns, and along the south shore.
Rightly, priority has been given to these "bread and butter" highways. The appropriate time for starting work on the Nova Scotia stretches of the Fundy trail will be when the major highway program has been completed and not before.
When one looks at the New Brunswick highways map it is immediately apparent that
December 16. 1968

only the southwestern part of the province has highways completed to modern standards, namely, the trans-Canada highway leading from the Quebec border through Woodstock, Fredericton, Moncton to the Nova Scotia border and also to the P.E.I. ferry crossing at Cape Tormentine. One finds also the highway, in part finished, from St. Stephen to Saint John, and the highway from Saint John to the main trans-Canada at Sussex. The highways just mentioned cover in part only the reauirement in the south and west areas. It will also be noticed that the eastern seaboard from Moncton to Caraquet and the northern part from Caraquet to Campbellton and then to St. Leonard, including villages too numerous to mention at this time, also the interior from Newcastle to Fredericton, are all served today by an arterial highway system far below the standards necessary to meet the present day traffic. These major arterial routes have the most basic effect upon economic development, and they constitute the highest priority for highway system development.
The effect of an adequate highway system on the cost of transportation with particular reference to railway freight charges was a subject of comment by the McPherson Royal Commission on Transportation. The report noted, and I quote:
Expansion of highways has not been uniformly extensive in all regions of Canada and this fact explains some of the disparities which exist in freight charges among regions. In recent years it has become characteristic of Canada's transportation system that areas which are most heavily populated and industrialized have been able to afford the development of highway networks which, with the accompanying growth of motor transport, has forced the railways to lower their rates in these areas in response to competition. At the same time, those regions less generously endowed with the prerequisites for the rapid growth of a highway system have experienced not only a relative absence of competitive railway rates but also the burden of an increasing share of those railway expenses which can no longer be obtained from rail revenues in the competitive sectors.
The Fundy trail, were it to be constructed, would be a scenic highway and, as it is generally known, highway construction is essentially a provincial responsibility. Simply because the Fundy trail would cross provincial boundaries and involve more than one province does not make it, ipso facto, a concern of the federal government. It would remain the responsibility of the two provinces concerned and if they wished to make it a joint provincial responsibility, that would be a matter for their determination.

Construction of Fundy Trail
The two provinces, like the federal government, have established priorities for spending, and the provinces know full well that the federal government has limited funds and that federal money expended on one project may mean that money is not to be available for another one. So it is understandable that neither province has yet approached the federal government to provide assistance for the construction of the Fundy trail.
The federal government, through the Department of Public Works and the Atlantic Development Board, has committed substantial sums of money for road and highway programs in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The development of these programs was in each case the consequence of joint federal-provincial planning which followed agreement on common priorities.
On November 4 of this year the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) announced in the house that under the trans-Canada Highway agreements construction in all provinces had already been approved for a total cost of $1,196 million of which amount $90,900,000 would be spent in Nova Scotia and $121,900,000 in New Brunswick. Thus far the federal government has actually expended $724,400,000 on the program; of this $60,900,900 was spent in Nova Scotia and $86,400,000 in New Brunswick. In other words, 20 per cent of all federal money expended on the trans-Canada highway has been spent in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, provinces which contain less than 7 per cent of the country's population.
The federal share in the whole program thus far represents a cost of about $58 per Canadian whereas the share of the federal program completed in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick represents a cost of almost twice that, $106 per resident. So looking at the federal government's involvement in the construction of the trans-Canada Highway in those two provinces, wherein the Fundy trail would run, it is obvious, no matter what basis of comparison is chosen, that relative to elsewhere in Canada the involvement is too high.
In summary, the Department of Public Works has spent $147,300,000 in the two provinces; committed and yet unspent by the department for the Trans-Canada Highway program is an additional $65,500,000.
Now let us turn to see the highway program of the Atlantic Development Board. In 1964, the A.D.B. initiated a program to upgrade and, in some cases, to construct main trunk highways in the four Atlantic provinces. Since that time the board has continued
4000	COMMONS
Construction of Fundy Trail and expanded this program. Costs have been shared with the provinces and while the relative shares have varied from agreement to agreement, the board has always borne 50 per cent or more of the costs. For the portion of the trunk highway program in Nova Scotia, the board has committed $19,500,000; a similar amount has been committed for New Brunswick. As of October 31, 1968, a total of $27,471,988 had been spent in the two provinces, $11,324,889 in Nova Scotia and $16,147,099 in New Brunswick.
In addition to its investment in highway and road programs being administered by the Department of Public Works and the Atlantic Development Board, the federal government has made further expenditures for the same purpose through some other departments. For example, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will see in this fiscal year the completion of the roads to resources program, a program of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Invested in each province, essentially for tourist roads, will be the sum of $7.5 million. Tourism is also being enhanced by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development through its program of building highways and access roads to serve the country's national parks. Not to be forgotten, either, is the Department of Transport which has also expended money on roads in the maritimes.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Instead of trying to recount every dollar spent by the government of Canada in the two provinces, I merely wished to demonstrate that the government has spent and is spending considerable amounts for road and highway construction there. Before the federal government even now, there is a joint submission from the four Atlantic provinces that the government contribute 90 per cent towards their ten year highway program, the total cost of which will be in excess of $900 million. It is against this backdrop of information that the proposal for additional funds for the Fundy trail must be viewed.
Having put on the record a brief outline of the federal effort in the construction of highways for New Brunswick, in comparison with other provinces, I think it would be of interest to see the provincial effort. The last fiscal year for which I have reliable statistics is 1966-67. In that year New Brunswick invested $75.90 per capita on the highway system, against an average expenditure by the other provinces of $50.57 per capita. New

DEBATES	December 16, 1968
Brunswick has the second highest per capita expenditure of all the provinces.
It may be of greater significance to consider the proportion of the provincial budget that is invested in the highway system. New Brunswick allocated to the highway system the highest percentage of net provincial budget of all Canadian provinces. I want to be very clear on this matter. I am discussing the expenditure of provincial dollars exclusive of federal contributions. During 1966-67 we spent 32.5 cents of every provincial dollar on the highway system. The average of the provinces to the west of New Brunswick was 16.7 cents, about one half of our investment.
I think I can say with some pride that the government of New Brunswick and its citizens have made a massive effort to solve our transportation problems and with the continuing co-operation that exists between the good offices of the federal and our provincial government I have full confidence that the people of New Brunswick will see these accomplishments realized, especially now that we have a federal minister and department charged with the responsibility of solving some of the problems in regions such as ours. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I will do everything possible on my part to work in complete co-operation with this minister, to see that this will be achieved.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to light an editorial from the Moncton Daily Times of April 26, 1968. It voices my sentiments with respect to one of my very good friends who was mentioned by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) and who is also mentioned in the editorial, and it says:
This newspaper is just as solidly in favour of the principle of the proposed Fundy trail as it ever was, but we feel that its cause was hindered rather than helped by the intemperate remarks made about New Brunswick highways minister Andre F. Richard by the general chairman of the Fundy trail committee, Mr. Mitchell Franklin of Saint John, during a meeting held in the Hillsborough regional High School on Tuesday night.
Use of such uncomplimentary terms as "stooge", "obstructionist", "saboteur", to describe an elected minister of the crown was highly uncalled for, to say the very least. Mr. Franklin is not helping to hasten the ultimate realization of the * Fundy trail project one little bit by resorting to tactics such as this. An approach of this kind could very well have the opposite effect-of causing the project to recede even farther into the future than it is now. Differences of opinion are one thing-the right to voice them is part and parcel of our free democratic process-but they should be tempered with much greater respect and understanding than was shown in this instance, if the right of free speech is to be kept on the high level plane that we have come to expect of our public speakers.
December 16, 1968	COMMONS
This newspaper is fully convinced, as is Hon. Mr. Richard too, that the construction of the Fundy trail along the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia shores of the bay of Fundy and the other bays leading into it is capable of conferring incalculable benefits upon the tourist trade of the maritime provinces. But this project is going to cost a very large sum of money, and after all, there is such a thing as priorities in this, as in many other things on which taxpayers' money could be spent.
The New Brunswick minister of highways never has come out in opposition to the Fundy trail- he has merely pointed out that his province, for the moment, has a large backlog of urgently needed, year-round highway construction projects that must be tackled quickly if this province is to progress economically in the manner in which it should. This project was brought forward some 20 or 25 years ago. Delegations came to Ottawa to discuss it. I recall that the first person who had a responsibility for and an interest in this was Hon. Milton F. Gregg, a minister of labour and minister of veterans affairs in those days. Since that time this matter has grown in interest and, as I say, has been debated, although perhaps not as extensively as it has been today. I believe it was debated mainly during consideration of the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which has the responsibility for national parks.
The reason I became interested in this is that in New Brunswick we have a very attractive national park. As everybody knows, it is one of the better family recreational parks in Canada, although it is small when compared with other national parks. I believe it is the second smallest in Canada. We feel that if we are to have the advantages which a national park of Canada should have, the boundary of the park must be increased. Alongside this park there is the land which has been referred to today. This is old timber land. However it has no further use as timber land, and has no other value in the foreseeable future.
This land could be added to the park without much difficulty or expense on the part of the provincial authorities. In that way the
December 16, 1968

Construction of Fundy Trail federal government would then become responsible for a highway or a trail through the park. In other words, we are not fighting over provincial moneys; nor are we talking about federal moneys that would otherwise go into highways in another manner. We are simply talking about extending the area of the park. In that way, with the resources available in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, a very substantial and inexpensive part of this highway could be built.
In all the time that I have debated this matter I have never said that the provincial government should provide $50 million of their very scarce highway funds for the building of a Fundy trail, or a super highway down the bay of Fundy. I hope this will be clear, because this misconception is the biggest red herring I have ever seen dragged around in a debate in my life. I think everyone agrees that this is a situation where the government should take some of the moneys available in different ways for park expansion, and use it for this purpose, so that so far as New Brunswick is concerned a very substantial part of the highway could be started.
This is a project which could be extended over the next 30, 40 or 50 years. It could be done in the same way the western parks were developed. We might ask how much money has gone into the parks of Jasper and Banff. Millions of dollars have gone into those parks, and they are beautiful. As Canadians we are proud of those parks. But I suggest we should do something like this in New Brunswick, and that is the reason I am supporting this measure.
Another misconception is that concerning the suggestion that this park, and the highway, would be used during a very short tourist season. I believe there is a very great future in New Brunswick in winter sports. Money is being spent for this purpose in many of our other national parks. It is being spent in the national park in Nova Scotia to develop opportunities for winter recreation. We believe that in New Brunswick we are entitled to have a full assessment of the skiing possibilities. An assessment was made in a minor way, but a complete assessment is necessary in respect of the Fundy National Park, and this should include the potential for winter activity. If this were done, it probably would be possible to make use of the park facilities which have been put there, and 
are now being developed by private enterprise. In this way the park could be used on a year around basis. The facilities which are there, and in many other parts of the area, could be developed.
I commend the hon. member who is new to the house for coming forward with this measure, one which would mean so much to his area and the southern part of New Brunswick. I believe he deserves great credit for standing up and putting this forward in the house. The hon. member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Crossman) is a good friend of mine, but I am sorry that he pulled this great red herring over the Fundy trail, because I think this is a project which can stand on its own four feet, without any of the bickering which goes on about it in the provincial legislature. That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of giving immediate consideration to the provision of special financial assistance to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia for the construction of the

Fundy trail from St. Stephen, New Brunswick to Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, using existing roads where possible, and assisting financially in connecting existing roads in order that a scenic highway be available to aid in the promotion of the tourist industry.
So, I think it is very clear that the question here is not in respect of a national park but of building a highway. The way in which I should like to approach this, first of all, is to agree with the hon. member for Moncton, that we should think about this from an industrial, and not necessarily from the highway point of view. First of all I must mention that, regardless of what else it is, the highway is still a public utility. It is still a means to an end; it is a highway to go to some place. [DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
The government has committed itself to an effort to activate the economy of New Brunswick and the other Atlantic provinces. That is the reason it is important to look at this from an industrial point of view. First of all, because of the amount of money involved, when we consider it from an industrial point of view we must look at the priorities. We must say, first of all, in respect of industrial development whether we should give special emphasis to tourism, secondary manufacturing, mining or to the fishing industry, which is in a difficult position today because of a poor market. I think all these things are important. We must decide within the promotion of industrial development where tourism stands. I have been in some areas where the tourist industry is very important; for example, California. The people do not go there only because there are good highways, they go because there are other attractions there.
I could mention such other areas as Nassau, Bermuda, Jamaica and Porto Rico. People do not go to those places because there are good highways. There must be other attractions for them. We build highways when we have excessive traffic; we do not build highways to create traffic.
I think the Fundy area is most inviting; it certainly is picturesque. If there is need of a highway, and there is an overflow of traffic through that area-and there might be one

Construction of Fundy Trail day-then I think we should consider building this highway. However, I do not think we should decide to build a highway only with the idea of promoting the tourist industry.
The hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) said that the Fundy trail would probably attract 200,000 tourists each year, but he has not said where he got this figure- whether it is a guess, the result of some economist's work, or a figure calculated by a specialist in the tourist industry. Perhaps it is a figure suggested by the people of the Fundy area; I do not know.
Let me point out that P.E.I. is a very attractive spot, one of the most beautiful islands in the world; yet it attracts less than 500,000 tourists a year. I wonder if this Fundy trail would attract that many tourists. Where would they come from? Would they be the tourists who now visit New Brunswick or those who visit the Cabot trail? I fail to see how the construction of this highway would bring 200,000 people to the area.
The hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) has suggest that this highway could be used all year round. I understand there are no hills in the area on which ski slopes could be developed. I do not understand why people would be attracted to go to the Fundy area in the wintertime, and I say this because I understand the tourist industry in New Brunswick is handicapped by a short season. There are only two months during which people would be attracted.
In the last few years the trend has been for people to travel with camping trailers. This trend has reduced the amount of revenue in any area, because people are not taking advantage of existing lodging facilities. If an area has a park which people visit, even though there may be a million people each year, how much revenue goes to that local area? New Brunswick, it has been suggested, obtains $77 million from tourists each year, and it is said, further, that Nova Scotia obtains $60 million. But to this point in the debate no one has said how much money is obtained by the local areas from tourism.
It may be that if we had this highway in the Fundy area we might have ten service stations, ten restaurants and ten motels or hotels. How much employment would this create? Some people might argue that the building of the road itself would create

Construction of Fundy Trail employment, but if we consider our experience we will realize that the major expenditures involved in highway construction can be related to the leasing of equipment, and the purchase of raw materials and finished materials. Very little goes to the local people. A few labourers would be hired, but from a construction point of view we cannot say this would create many jobs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great feeling that I enter this debate. Being a new member and backbencher, I have listened to the debate with great interest. When the people of Marquette constituency sent me to Ottawa as their representative, I came here with great expectations and hope that this was to be the beginning of the just society, the beginning of a new era for Canada and Canadians. After the report of the procedure committee and the proposals of the government, I am alarmed and disillusioned, not only for the future of Canada but for the future of the House of Commons. We all realize that certain reforms have to be made in the House of Commons. All parties and members agree with this. But the extent to which the government proposes to change the rules is, I believe, an infringement of the rights of members of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I will mention the points which concern me. I appeal to the backbenchers on the government side to consider seriously the implications of these proposals. It has been pointed out that the government house leader could limit the debate to two
[Mr. Breau.l
December 16, 1968
hours. I found it most interesting when the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) was asked whether, if a bill affecting mining in his area came up, he would be able to participate if there was a two-hour limit on debate. The hon. member was certain that through the good will of the government he would be allowed to participate in the debate. I ask: What would happen if the bill affected all mining areas of Canada, which would mean that the ridings of many members would be affected and they might want to speak? This would be impossible with a two-hour time limit. It will be said that these members could speak out at committee. This sounds good; but, Mr. Speaker, my experience with committee meetings is that often two or three committees are meeting at once-I mean committees which affect one's riding-and it is impossible to attend them all. In my short time here this situation has arisen more than once.
There is another point which alarms me about committees. We know a member can attend any committee meeting he chooses. However if he is not a member of the committee he can ask questions, but he cannot vote. Under this plan I feel that my constituency, or any constituency, is being discriminated against, because if these proceedings were left in the house any member could participate in the debate and vote. Again I stress that I am in favour of reform. But where does it stop?
This government is continually shrugging off the rights of opposition members. During this session we have had the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) introduce his now famous roster system for the presence of ministers in the house during the daily question period. Hardly a week goes by when it is not pointed out that this system is not only unfair but is not working; yet the Prime Minister will not change it. Originally he said we would try this idea to see how it worked. Any time he was questioned about it, we were given a shrug of the shoulders and a flippant answer.
I remind backbenchers on the other side of the house that some day they will be in opposition and will find how frustrating it is to want to raise an important question, which requires an answer that day, only to find that they cannot ask it because it is not the ministers day designated to be in the house. Or maybe it is a Friday, and because you cannot get the Speaker's attenion-and I fully realize the problems the Speaker faces in this regard -you are not able to put the question. Quite
Motion for Concurrence in Report often it is the following Wednesday before the particular minister is in the house. This means it has taken six days to get an answer to your question, when it should have been given the day the question was asked. Yet, Mr. Speaker, this roster system continues.
This session started off with the Prime Minister silencing his cabinet ministers. Next the government set up the roster system for the attendance of ministers. The next step was for the Prime Minister to bypass his own members and set up his own lines of communication or, as the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) called them, Trudeau's snoop troops. Now the Prime Minister wants to silence the opposition. Where is all this leading? I ask, what will be next? With the growth of staff in this government, and the number of executive assistants overflowing into the diplomatic gallery, perhaps the next step will be that the government will take over the press gallery.
Again I stress that we are in favour of reform; but we are not in favour of proposed rule 16-A. Rule 16-A would allow the government house leader to say how long any debate would run, and this is against our whole democratic system. Could we on this basis operate our school boards, our municipal, our councils, our church groups, our service clubs or any organizations which are so much a part of our life? They could not operate on this basis, and neither can parliament.
Mr. Speaker, during this debate hon. members on the government side have said that the opposition are holding up legislation. As an example, they claim that the three agriculture bills took three weeks to pass in the house. Why did they take three weeks? It was because the government would not bend in any way or allow amendments to those bills. What kind of bills did we end up with? The number of complaints I have received with regard to cash advances on farm stored grain confirms that this new act discriminates against the small farmer on a six bushel quota. We repeatedly asked the government to tell us the interest rates under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Credit Corporation Act, but it replied that these rates would be set by governor in council and we need not worry. We now have the new interest rates. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act the interest rate went from 5 per cent to per cent, and under the Farm Credit Corporation Act it went from 5 per cent to 7| per cent. If the government members think this is good legislation, I ask

December 16, 1968

Motion for Concurrence in Report them to come with me to western Canada and talk to the farmers, and they will soon find out what the farmers think of the legislation.
I maintain that if any government proposes good legislation, and the opposition delays it by needless debate, the Canadian voters will pass judgment at the next election. My point is that if the government presents good legislation it will pass in any parliament with limited debate. The Prime Minister says we are not in touch with the people, and the people want parliamentary reform. I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Brandon Sun of September 12 this year. It shows the concern of people over the proposed rules changes. I quote from this newspaper as follows:
In addition, however, there are rather alarming reports about government efforts to streamline house procedures. Without question procedures sorely need streamlining, but if reports such as that carried earlier in the week by Peter Newman are accurate, the government is carrying things too far.
It must be remembered that parliament is moving into a new phase, a phase of majority government for the first time in over five years. Some restrictions on debate which were considered necessary during the period of minority government are potentially dangerous when the government is in a strong majority position. The opposition can no longer defeat the government. Therefore its only weapon is debate, debate aimed at bringing government misdeeds to the attention of the public. In a very real sense the public must be a check on the government, and the opposition represents a sizeable percentage of the public.
The new rules have not been made public. When they are. they should be examined carefully. Efficiency at the expense of full discussion should not be parliament's goal.

I think this point deserves serious thought. Judging from my short experience here in the house it would seem to me that it cannot be done.
May I stress again that we are in favour of procedural reforms, but we do not support rule 16-A. Government members say the voters have given them a mandate and they are a majority government. [Mr. Stewart (Marquette) .1

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Marquette on having made his maiden speech on such a very important issue as the change in rules which will affect our parliamentary life in the period ahead. I think he has made his points very clearly and strongly, and his speech, I believe, has been typical of the speeches made in this debate and in the debate which is going on in the press throughout the country. I have been impressed by the sober and temperate tone used both in the house and throughout the country, because I believe there must have been a temptation to make sensational reading out of some of this material; yet this temptation has not been yielded to. I think people realize that this is a very serious matter and that we should be careful to deal with it responsibly.
It is not my intention tonight to make a detailed analysis of the rule changes in the proposal now before us, and for two reasons. First, this has already been done exhaustively and well, and I think we know now what the significance of the proposed changes is likely to be. Furthermore these proposed changes have been explained to us in the house by the best legal and constitutional minds here, and they in turn have cited other authorities
December 16, 1968	COMMONS
along legal, constitutional and historical lines.
I want to say how much a great many of us appreciated the speech made by the hon. member for Funay-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) this afternoon, a speech which was philosophical and historical and at the same time reflected a great depth of thought, and much reading and consideration of this whole problem.
Nor do I think there is any need to take up time justifying the necessity for updating the rules of parliament. All of us here, even those who have sat here for only a few months since the opening of this parliament, have become convinced of the need for change and of the fact that the machinery of parliament should be updated, and made more streamlined and more efficient. So I do not think there can be any argument on that point. Where the argument comes in is as to the method in which this updating and streamlining is to be carried out.
We in the opposition parties are of one mind. This may seem strange because we are not of one mind on a great many other methods of getting things done. But in this particular matter we feel sure that any changes, if they are to preserve the democratic character of this parliament, can be made only by agreement and consent of all parties in this chamber. Unfortunately the attitude of the government has been that they will listen to what we have to say, but then they will make up their minds; and we will have to take it because they have what it takes to make us swallow the new rules, whether we want to or not. We do not think that this is the way to make changes in a democratic parliament.
Somebody has already pointed out in this debate that there are two ways of achieving a totalitarian form of government, a one party monolithic government. One way is to ban all the parties but one. The other way is to permit the members of the parties to be elected to parliament, and then either to gag them at once, or gradually take away their facilities for expression and for bringing their constituents' ideas before the body of the house.
I believe that this is the method being followed in these proposed rule changes. We on the opposition side agree that this should not be done. There are two alternatives: Either the government believes that these rule changes should be forced upon parliament to make parliament work more effectively, or else they are trying to force them on parliament in order to bypass parliament altogether. We believe that the effect of forcing these changes on parliament will be to enable the
DEBATES	4007
Motion for Concurrence in Report government to bypass parliament altogether. We do not believe that this is permissible, and we would not be doing our duty as members of this house, we, who have had these democratic privileges handed to us, if we did not ensure that the essence of democracy is handed on to other people who will sit in this parliament long after we are gone.
The effect of rule 16-A is to bypass parliament. In the first place it gives the government the power to dictate to parliament because it gives them the power to enforce closure ahead of time. I would like to remind hon. members opposite of what happened in 1956 when, in the infamous pipe line debate, closure was applied, not before the debate began but after it had proceeded only a little way. When that happened, to put it in the simplest and most expressive language possible, all hell broke loose and parliament determined henceforth that it would not suffer again that crippling blow to parliamentary privileges.
The effect of the application of closure was to put the then existing government out of power. I want to warn this government that should it be so foolish as to insist on doing the same thing again only in an even more objectionable form, on applying closure before we even start the debate, the same fate will again overtake this government, because no democracy-loving people will put up with it.

When the proposed rule 16-A is coupled with other developments that we have seen take place this fall, then I think the situation becomes ominous. For example, reference has been made to the roster system. What is the
December 16, 1968

Motion for Concurrence in Report roster system? It has the effect of removing on most of the days of the parliamentary week about half of the cabinet ministers, with the result that about half of the subjects which are raised receive no answer. The worst feature is that the only day on which we do have access to all the members of the cabinet is the short day in the middle of the week with the half hour question period. Mr. Speaker and hon. members, this has been a good debate and I think it has proceeded in the best tradition of parliament. We have heard excellent cases put forward by those speaking on all sides of this extremely important and urgent matter of procedure. I think in the main the views expressed have been responsible views.
I speak as one with a good deal of experience in opposition. I served in one of the most interesting legislatures in Canada for a period of nine years, at times under difficult circumstances. My experience on the opposition "barbed wire" was trying at times. I think I am as aware as any member of this house of the value and the necessity of good responsible opposition. I will not be party to any action by any government here now or in the future, to take away from the opposition its rights and responsibilities under our great parliamentary traditions. Without good and effective opposition, governments degenerate and deteriorate. They have in the past. The opposition is an integral and important element in the constitutional organization of parliament. As a former prime minister, the right hon. member for Prince Albert, said on October 27, 1949, in a most excellent speech with reference to the responsibilities of the opposition-and this is set out at page 69 of the text:
"When it properly discharges them the preservation of our freedom is assured. The reading of history proves that freedom always dies when criticism ends. It upholds and maintains the rights of minorities against majorities. It must be vigilant against oppression and unjust invasions by the cabinet of the rights of the people. It should supervise all expenditures and prevent over-expenditure by exposing to the light of public opinion wasteful expenditures or worse. It finds fault; it suggests amendments; it asks questions and elicits information; it arouses, educates and moulds public opinion by voice and vote. It must scrutinize every action by the government and in doing so prevents the shortcuts through democratic procedure that governments like to make."

HIGHWAY SAFETY-INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week or two ago on orders of the day I attempted to raise the question of tire safety in Canada, as this relates to the general question of automotive safety in Canada and the United States. At that time Mr. Speaker ruled my question out of order and I take the opportunity of discussing it again now. My question was and is prompted by the fact that whereas in the United States a good deal of attention is being paid to tire standards and specifications, to the retreading of tires and the grooving of bus, school bus and truck tires, with proper standards and specifications being established, so far as I know in Canada there is no bureau of tire standards. We have no specifications setting out what must be the quality of retreads and grooved tires.
4022	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion [DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
For quite some time now I have been interested in the whole question of traffic safety involving, as it does, the standardization of the quality of car parts and car repairs. The entire subject is currently under review in the United States by a senate subcommittee, and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs told us the other day that similar action might be taken here. I think we are living dangerously in Canada when we neglect to establish proper standards for tire safety, or to make adequate provision for tire safety checks and call-backs when tires are found to be faulty, as is the case in the United States should tires be found wanting after a safety inspection has been carried out.
When it comes to tire safety I think we depend too much on what our United States friends are exporting into this country. Tires are checked there to the extent I have indicated, but we do not provide our own Canadian standards, although we certainly have our own geographic and climatic conditions which affect tires used here.
Tire safety is just one aspect of automotive safety. Every week in the past few years at least 100 Canadians died on our roads and highways. Some 3,000 are injured, many of them to the extent that they might as well be dead. In economic terms, the toll runs to $600 million a year, including car insurance.
In the relatively short period of six years during which I have been a member of this house, 30,000 Canadians have died in traffic accidents and 950,000 have been injured. The economic loss amounts to more than four billion dollars. Mr. Speaker, this is a very warlike total, and tire safety, or rather the lack of tire safety provisions, is one of the reasons for these alarming figures.
My question was, in effect: "Having in mind reports concerning tires which were given safety tests in the United States and which failed such tests, and in view of the fact that some of these tires are imported into Canada, I want to ask when we are to have a testing bureau for tire safety with a system of call-backs for tires proven faulty?"

The company's statement appeared to catch the smaller companies by surprise.
B.C. Telephone said it had no plans to seek rate increases. New Brunswick Telephone said it also has no such plans-
Maritime Telegraph and Telephone Co. Ltd. of Halifax has not applied for an increase in its rates, although the company faces the same factors that prompted Bell to seek an increase, according to D. W. Myers, Maritime's vice president and general manager-
Quebec Telephone refused to comment on whether the company plans to seek rate increases.
There you have it, Mr. Speaker, that many of the other telephone companies within Canada had not planned on making applications for any rate increases.
Bell Telephone Company officials say the new rates are necessary to improve the company's financial position and its abilities to raise capital. The increase of 10 per cent would bring Bell $80 million, and if in effect for all of 1969 the company's return on invested capital would be 8 per cent.
We should also note that so far as this year's earnings are concerned analysts are estimating $3.25 to $3.30 a share, as compared with $3.16 in 1967. It is obvious that they are not anticipating any loss or any reduction in the earnings on their share capital.
Bell Telephone claims it will need $180 million in external financing in 1969, and if it were to go to the market for debt money it would have to pay around 8 per cent. Since 1967 Bell has raised $287 million by bond financing and its rates have ranged from 6.25 per cent to 7f per cent. The most recent was this summer's $75 million issue in U.S. funds with interest at 6.9 per cent. Bell's over-all debt service cost is still below 6.2 per cent.

A few weeks ago on the program "Twenty Million Questions" the Postmaster General was asked questions concerning the communication systems in Canada, and in reply to a question by Mr. Jones he said:
Well I think the problem that worries me the most is probably the international law aspects of communications; and secondarily the federal-provincial relations aspects of it. To go the second one first,-you know we have control over,- although I don't think the regulations are all that good,-over the Bell Telephone and the B.C. Telephone, but not over provincial telephone companies.
So you can see the Postmaster General is concerned about this communications problem and the regulations controlling this particular company.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The time has come for the government to do a study in depth to determine whether the Bell Telephone Company should come under public ownership. The main purpose of the Bell Telephone Company should be to provide the best available telephone service at the lowest possible rate. Telephone service should not depend on satisfying 250,000 shareholders that they are receiving a high return on their invested capital or the necessity of paying high interest rates on bonds for expansion capital. This is the reason many Canadians would like a government feasibility study of public ownership of our communications system.
If the Canadian Development Corporation had been set up and functioning Bell Telephone ownership by the corporation would at least have spread ownership to many more Canadians. Therefore I should like the Postmaster General to state whether the government is opposing the application by the Bell Telephone Company for the rate increase and whether the minister would announce the setting up of a task force to study the feasibility of public ownership of this company which is now operating for the benefit of only a few and certainly not all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, for an opening remark, I think I can only repeat what I said before; that is, the Canadian Transport Commission is a quasi judicial body empowered to make its own decisions. Neither the government nor the minister of communications has any right or power to intervene in the judgment of the C.T.C. This is the reason it was set up. While I do not doubt the figures of the hon. member, I think that while they may have an

This is not said in any way to justify their decision to make the application at this time.
The hon. member, however, has raised an important point. The decision of the C.T.C. will be based, naturally, upon the information made available to it. To me the major issue that is raised is how complete will be the information that will be made public by the telephone company. In this regard the hon. member made reference to some doubt I have expressed about the completeness of information that we presently have. I should like to confirm that statement and say that on the basis of a preliminary assessment by my department much more information will be necessary in the future than heretofore.
The present information is insufficient for the department of communications, a department which as hon. members know is in the process of being established. Why? The function and the mandate of the department of communications it to create a national program and a national policy of telecommunications. We can only do that job if we have the necessary tools, and the essential tool is information on the state of Canada's telecommunications industry, the entire industry. I repeat that I do not believe we now have the information we need to make wise economic, technological and sociological decisions for the maximum benefit of the Canadian public. I say this not intending any inference in respect of the information before the C.T.C. to which the hon. member referred. This information will be judged upon its own intrinsic merits in respect of the long term development of communications in this country.
For that objective, and I am choosing my words with care, I intend to do everything necessary to ensure that the department of communications will be able to command the tools and have the information it needs to make a complete audit of the economic and financial fabric of Canadian telecommunications. Once that inventory is completed we can proceed to make rational decisions on telecommunications development. I am certain that with co-operation we will be able to obtain and compile that information and inventory. At any rate I can assure hon. members that I intend to spare no effort to make sure that the inventory is compiled.

maintopic: SPORTS-HOCKEY-INTERFERENCE WITH FREEDOM OF CHOICE OF YOUNG PLAYERS
SPORTS-HOCKEY-INTERFERENCE WITH FREEDOM OF CHOICE OF YOUNG PLAYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question arises tonight, addressed to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and involves a complaint I have had from my riding, specifically from Stoney Creek, Ontario. It arises from a letter I received from one Karl Beckwick, Stoney Creek and dated December 3, 1968 in which he says:
Dear Sir:
It was suggested to me by John McLellan, a neighbour, to write a letter to you. Apparently my boy, Jim, is in the same predicament as young Frank McLellan.
We were informed in a letter from the Ontario Minor Hockey Assoc., that Jim can no longer play hockey for the Saltfleet team-
This is a ridiculous situation. Jim has played for Saltfleet for four years. We still reside at 15 Durham Road. There has been no amalgamation or annexation of our area, and certainly the Salt-fleet club has not released Jim.
It escapes me, why, all of a sudden there are changes made by the Ontario Minor Hockey Assoc., after the boy has become so well established with his home club. I can't see how he can be forced to play for a strange club, and leave all his friends that he has skated with and gone to school with all these years. It is preposterous.
Recently there have been a number of this type of complaint received from this area. It has been widespread that throughout Canada the tentacles of professional sports organizations and commercial enterprises are creeping in to take control of boys of school age, who should be getting the opportunity to play amateur hockey. We will never really get a well trained team in this country, and we will never be able to develop our youth with the proper spirit of sports when this type of practice is widespread.
It appears the coaches of some of these teams have been notified by the president of the Ottawa Minor Hockey Association that certain boys are prohibited from playing for their home teams. The parents of these boys strenuously object on their behalf and I protest on their behalf this unwarranted interference with a boy's right to play for his home team, in this case Stoney Creek or Saltfleet. Is this not a matter which should be investigated by the task force on amateur sports? If anyone questions the constitutionality of this matter I submit it is an example of professional control of amateur sports. When this matter is investigated in detail it will become quite apparent that this is what has happened.
December 16, 1S68

I am suspicious of the monopolistic control of amateur sport by commercial interests. We will never get a world championship hockey team by destroying the free right to choose a team, and by stifling the spirit of these boys. There is far too much interference by commercial groups with the careers and rights of these boys in Canada, and I believe an inquiry by the task force will bring out into the open the nature and extent of this abuse. Can we not free the boys from this power? I ask the minister to make an investigation into this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the comments of the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Gibson), one would think that he plays on the same team as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). I should like to reassure the hon. member by quoting some remarks the hon. minister made in Moncton on November 23, 1968 when he was talking about the need to give a new status to amateur sports. I quote:
These measures include several changes. First of all, if professionals really want to respect
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
such a system of hockey, they must let each player decide for himself whether he wants to play on a national or an amateur team, such as a university team, for example, and how long he wants to be a part of that system. Consequently, they must stop pressing the young to enter a professional league at the earliest opportunity, and that means they must stop any pressure they apply during the whole school year.
Any premature signing of contracts, whether public or private, must cease. Businessmen cannot be permitted to buy and sell young athletes as if they were real estate. Hockey players are not chattels.
I want to assure the hon. member that this very problem is on the agenda of the task force. Meetings have taken place between the task force and the amateur and professional hockey associations and all those interested in this problem on a national level.
A report by the task force is expected early next year. I think their recommendations will contribute to raise our national and amateur sport to Olympic standing which will make us proud while it will respect the freedom of the people.
